pt.question: O LSA OSPFv2 Type 2 (Network) é gerado por quem e descreve o quê?
options: Cada router, os seus links P2P
O DR do segmento multiacesso, a lista de routers no segmento e a máscara
pt.explanation: Type 2 só existe onde há DR (broadcast/NBMA). O Link ID é o IP da interface do DR. Em point-to-point não há Type 2. Type 1 descreve os links do próprio router.

pt.question: Para que serve o LSA Type 4 (ASBR-summary)?
options: Permitir que routers noutras áreas saibam como alcançar um ASBR (Router ID do ASBR, gerado pelo ABR)
Substituir o Type 5 dentro da NSSA
pt.explanation: Type 5 tem o prefixo externo mas o next-hop de forwarding pode ser um ASBR noutra área. Type 4 dá o custo até esse ASBR. Em NSSAs o Type 5 não entra: usa-se Type 7, traduzido para 5 no ABR.

pt.question: Uma área OSPF totally stubby (no-summary) bloqueia o quê, relativamente a uma stub simples?
options: Além dos Type 4/5, também os Type 3 de summary; o ABR injeta apenas um default Type 3
pt.explanation: Stub: sem Type 5 (nem Type 4). Totally stubby: também sem Type 3 específicos, só default. NSSA: permite Type 7 redistribuídos. Totally NSSA: NSSA + no-summary. Área de transit (0) nunca é stub.

pt.question: Quando se usa um virtual-link OSPF?
options: Para ligar uma área discontiguous à área 0 (ou costurar área 0 partida) através de uma área de transit não-stub
pt.explanation: Toda a área deve tocar na backbone. Virtual-link é um túnel lógico entre ABRs através de uma área regular. Não atravessa stub/NSSA. A solução limpa é redesenhar para que a área 0 seja contígua.

pt.question: O que é Stuck-in-Active (SIA) no EIGRP?
options: O router ficou Active à espera de replies a um Query e o SIA-timer expirou sem resposta de um vizinho
pt.explanation: Sem FS, DUAL envia Queries. Se um vizinho não responde (WAN má, MTU, CPU), o router declara SIA e reset a adjacência com esse peer. Mitigação: stub, summarization, SIA-timer, boa estabilidade de links.

pt.question: O que faz um router EIGRP configurado como stub connected summary?
options: Anuncia apenas connected e summary e não é consultado com Queries para destinos além do stub (reduz SIA)
pt.explanation: EIGRP stub é para sucursais: o hub não envia Queries para o stub a perguntar por redes do core. receive-only/static/redistributed são variantes. Não é o mesmo que OSPF stub.

pt.question: Os K-values EIGRP têm de coincidir entre vizinhos. O default clássico usa quais K?
pt.explanation: Métrica clássica ≈ 256 * (10^7/min_bw + sum_delay). K2 (load) e K4/K5 (reliability) não entram no default. Wide metrics (named mode) usam 64 bits. K mismatch = sem adjacência.

pt.question: No BGP, um MED (metric) menor significa o quê, e onde se compara?
options: Pior caminho; compara-se sempre entre ASes diferentes sem exceção
Melhor caminho; compara-se entre rotas do mesmo AS vizinho (salvo bgp always-compare-med)
pt.explanation: MED é opcional non-transitive. O default Cisco só compara MED de paths do mesmo neighbor AS. always-compare-med compara entre ASes (pode causar loops se não for consistente). Missing MED trata-se como 0 por omissão (bgp bestpath med missing-as-worst inverte).

pt.question: Para que serve AS-path prepend no BGP?
options: Encurtar o path para ganhar sempre
Anunciar o prefixo com o próprio AS repetido, tornando o path mais longo para os vizinhos e desviando entrada
pt.explanation: Prepend é engenharia de tráfego inbound barata. Local Pref/Weight controlam saída. Communities (no-export, local-AS) são mais limpas em escala. Não viola o AS, só alonga.

pt.question: Porque se configura neighbor x.x.x.x next-hop-self em iBGP num PE/edge?
options: Para que o next-hop dos prefixos eBGP passados a iBGP seja um endereço alcançável no IGP do AS (o próprio speaker)
pt.explanation: eBGP deixa o next-hop no peer externo, muitas vezes não resolvível no core. next-hop-self reescreve para o peering iBGP (loopback). Em RR aplica-se aos clientes. Alternativa: anunciar o /32 do next-hop externo no IGP (não costuma ser desejável).

pt.question: A community well-known no-export significa o quê?
options: Não anunciar o prefixo a nenhum iBGP
Não anunciar o prefixo para fora do AS (nem confederação para eBGP 'verdadeiro')
pt.explanation: no-export: fica no AS. no-advertise: não anunciar a nenhum peer. local-AS: não sair da sub-AS de confederação. Internet (default) pode ir a toda a gente. Communities são o gancho de policy do ISP.

pt.question: Qual é a diferença entre um route reflector e uma confederação BGP?
options: RR relaxa o split-horizon iBGP num cluster (clientes/non-clients); confederação parte o AS em sub-ASes com eBGP especial entre elas
pt.explanation: Ambos evitam o full mesh iBGP. RR é mais simples (cluster-id, originator-id contra loops). Confederação (64512-65534 privadas) isola policy por sub-AS e usa next-hop/MED como eBGP entre sub-ASes. Podem combinar-se.

pt.question: O que é eBGP multihop?
options: Permitir sessão eBGP entre endereços que não são diretamente adjacentes, subindo o TTL (omissão eBGP TTL=1)
pt.explanation: Típico: peering entre loopbacks através de um IGP/connected compartilhado, ou peering por vários hops. disable-connected-check cobre o caso loopback no mesmo link. Risco: TTL grande alarga a superfície; BFD ainda é recomendado.

pt.question: Numa MPLS L3VPN, PHP (penultimate hop popping) ocorre onde?
options: No router imediatamente antes do PE de egress, que faz pop da etiqueta de transporte (LDP/SR)
pt.explanation: O LSP de transporte é LDP (ou SR). O penúltimo hop faz pop para o PE de egress olhar só para a etiqueta VPN (ou IP em PHP+explicit-null variações). explicit-null preserva EXP/TTL até ao egress.

pt.question: LDP vs RSVP-TE em MPLS: qual contraste correto?
options: LDP estabelece LSPs segundo a RIB IGP, hop-by-hop; RSVP-TE sinaliza tunnels com restrições de banda/caminho
pt.explanation: LDP anda ao lado do IGP (lib/hello UDP 646, sessão TCP 646). RSVP-TE (e SR-TE) serve engenharia: bandwidth, affinity, fast reroute. Muitos cores misturam LDP no access e TE no backbone, ou passam a Segment Routing.

pt.question: BFD echo mode versus asynchronous: qual a ideia?
options: Async: os dois peers enviam control packets; Echo: o peer faz loopback do pacote echo do iniciador na forwarding path
Echo substitui o IGP por completo
pt.explanation: Echo testa o data plane do vizinho com menos CPU no peer. Nem todos os hardware/IOS suportam echo. Timers 50x3 ms são comuns em LAN; WAN usa valores mais conservadores. BFD e IGP/BGP ligam-se com 'fall-over bfd' / 'bfd all-interfaces'.

pt.question: Em PBR, qual é a diferença entre set ip next-hop e set interface?
options: set ip next-hop usa um IP (com fallback para routing normal se inalcançável, salvo default); set interface força a saída por essa iface (perigoso em multiacesso sem ARP)
set interface só funciona com BGP
set ip next-hop ignora a ACL do route-map
pt.explanation: PBR (ip policy route-map) casa ACLs/length/DSCP e desvia antes da RIB. set ip next-hop verify-availability + tracking/BFD evita blackhole. set ip default next-hop só se a RIB não tiver rota (exceto default).

pt.question: Num vPC Nexus, para que servem o peer-link e o peer-keepalive?
options: Peer-link sincroniza estado (MCS, LACP, IGMP, BPDUs) entre os dois peers; keepalive (link separado, mgmt) deteta dual-active se o peer-link falhar
Keepalive encaminha o tráfego de data plane dos servidores
pt.explanation: Os servers veem um EtherChannel para dois chassis. Sem keepalive, um peer-link down pode levar a split-brain (ambos active). Orphan ports são portas que só ligam a um peer. STP é filtrado de forma especial no vPC.

pt.question: O que é uma orphan port num vPC?
options: Uma porta LACP bundled nos dois peers
Uma porta que liga um dispositivo apenas a um dos switches vPC, não ao par
pt.explanation: Se o peer onde a orphan está falha, o dispositivo perde conectividade mesmo que o vPC do outro lado esteja up. Mitigação: dual-attach (vPC) ou orphan-port suspend. Peer-gateway / orphan-port podem ser necessários para routed traffic.

pt.question: No LISP usado pelo SD-Access, o Map-Server/Map-Resolver faz o quê?
options: Encapsula VXLAN no data plane de todos os edges
Control plane: guarda mapeamentos EID→RLOC e responde a Map-Requests dos ITR/ETR (edges)
pt.explanation: ITR pergunta 'onde está este EID?'; MS/MR (control plane node) responde o RLOC do ETR. Data plane é VXLAN (UDP 4789) entre RLOCs. Border nodes ligam o fabric ao resto da rede.

pt.question: Qual porta UDP usa o VXLAN no data plane?
pt.explanation: VXLAN usa UDP 4789 (IANA). CAPWAP usa 5246/5247. BGP 179. LDP 646. O VNI de 24 bits identifica o segmento no header VXLAN; EVPN (BGP AF) distribui MAC/IP (RT-2) e prefixos (RT-5).

pt.question: SGT inline versus SXP no TrustSec/ISE: qual a diferença?
options: SXP encapsula VXLAN; inline usa RADIUS
Inline transporta o tag no CMD/Cisco Meta Data do frame hop-by-hop; SXP (TCP 64999) propaga IP-SGT out-of-band onde o média não carrega o tag
pt.explanation: ISE classifica o utilizador e manda o SGT ao NAD (802.1X). Switches capable reencaminham o tag. SXP preenche gaps (WAN, terceiros). Enforcement: SGACL no destino. pxGrid partilha contexto com firewalls.

pt.question: O datastore candidate do NETCONF serve para quê?
options: Substituir o running imediatamente sem lock
Editar uma config proposta (edit-config) e depois commit atómico para running, com lock e rollback
pt.explanation: candidate + commit permite validar e aplicar tudo-ou-nada (confirmed-commit com rollback automático). running-only devices editam direto. RESTCONF tem o mesmo modelo YANG mas HTTP. Confirmed commit é o antídoto a lockouts de AAA/ACL.

pt.question: DMVPN Phase 1 versus Phase 3: qual contraste correto?
options: Phase 1 é hub-and-spoke (spokes não constroem túneis entre si); Phase 3 usa NHRP redirect/shortcut para spoke-to-spoke
pt.explanation: Phase 2 permite spoke-to-spoke mas com tabelas de routing full nos spokes (summaries no hub quebram). Phase 3: hub manda NHRP redirect, spokes instalam shortcut; summaries no hub funcionam. IPsec profile + mGRE + NHRP são comuns às fases.

pt.question: No GETVPN, quais são os papéis de Key Server (KS) e Group Member (GM)?
options: KS encaminha o data plane; GM só faz IGP
KS distribui SA de grupo (GDOI/IKEv1) aos GMs; os GMs cifram o tráfego original preservando IP header (tunnel-less) na WAN privada
pt.explanation: GETVPN (GDOI) serve WANs MPLS/privadas onde o header IP original deve permanecer para routing. TBAR (time-based anti-replay) e COOP KS (redundância) são típicos. Não substitui DMVPN na Internet pública (não há túnel/NAT traversal de grupo).

pt.question: CoPP versus CPPr (Control Plane Protection): qual a nuance?
options: São nomes do mesmo feature sem diferença
CoPP aplica um policy-map à interface lógica control-plane (agregado); CPPr (host/transit/cef-exception) subdivide o CEF para granularidade extra no IOS clássico
pt.explanation: Ambos protegem a CPU de floods (TTL expiry, ICMP, SSH). Comece por copiar a policy Cisco-recommended e afinar. Undercopping quebra BGP/OSPF; overpermitting deixa o DoS entrar. NX-OS usa copp profile.

pt.question: uRPF strict versus loose: qual a diferença?
options: Loose exige que a origem case a interface de entrada; strict só pede existência na FIB
Strict: o reverse path da origem tem de apontar para a interface de entrada; loose: basta a origem existir na FIB (qualquer iface), útil em assimetria
pt.explanation: ip verify unicast source reachable-via rx = strict; reachable-via any = loose. Strict é o anti-spoofing forte em access; loose no edge com routing assimétrico. allow-default e ACL de exceção afinam o comportamento.

pt.question: Em PIM-SM num segmento multiacesso, o Designated Router (DR) serve para quê?
options: Enviar Register para o RP (fontes) e Join/Prune em nome dos receivers locais (IGMP)
pt.explanation: O DR PIM (maior IP, ou prioridade) é o único a registar fontes e a enviar joins para o RP. Não confundir com DR OSPF. Assert elege o forwarder quando há vários routers com o mesmo grupo na LAN.

pt.question: Qual é o contraste entre Auto-RP e BSR para descoberta de RP?
options: BSR é Cisco-only; Auto-RP é IETF
Auto-RP (Cisco, 224.0.1.39/40) anuncia RPs via mapping agent; BSR (RFC, mensagens PIM) elege um Bootstrap Router que difunde o RP-set
pt.explanation: Auto-RP precisa que os sparse-dense ou auto-rp listener permitam os grupos 39/40. BSR é padrão e atravessa PIM-SM nativo. Anycast-RP (MSDP ou RFC 4610) dá redundância geográfica do RP.

pt.question: O que é o SPT switchover no PIM-SM?
options: Depois de receber o primeiro pacote via shared tree (*,G) rumo ao RP, o last-hop DR pode enviar (S,G) Join direto à fonte, abandonando o RP no caminho
pt.explanation: O default Cisco faz switchover imediato (spt-threshold 0). spt-threshold infinity mantém o tráfego no shared tree (útil se a fonte é breve). SSM (IGMPv3, 232/8) vai direto (S,G) sem RP.

pt.question: IS-IS em campus/WAN ENCOR: L1 versus L2 significa o quê?
options: L1 é eBGP; L2 é iBGP
L1 é intra-área (estação); L2 é backbone entre áreas; L1/L2 vive na fronteira e faz route leaking do default
pt.explanation: IS-IS não usa área 0 à la OSPF: o backbone é o conjunto de routers L2 contíguos. NET (área + SysID + NSEL). Métrica wide é obrigatória em redes modernas. IS-IS é base habitual de SR/LDP em SP.

pt.question: OSPFv3 Address Families (AF) no IOS-XE permitem o quê?
options: Só um processo IPv6 clássico sem IPv4
Um processo OSPFv3 a transportar IPv6 e/ou IPv4 (AFs), com adjacências ainda em link-local
pt.explanation: OSPFv3 clássico era só IPv6. AF (RFC 5838) leva IPv4 sobre OSPFv3. Adjacências continuam IPv6 link-local; router-id ainda é IPv4 de 32 bits. Instance ID separa AFs.

pt.question: IPv6 RA Guard no acesso serve para quê?
options: Impedir que um host malicioso anuncie Router Advertisements e se faça passar por gateway IPv6
pt.explanation: RA Guard (e DHCPv6 Guard, ND inspection) são First-Hop Security. Portas de acesso: host-mode (RAs drop). Uplinks para routers: router-mode. Sem isto, um RA falso desvia o tráfego IPv6.

pt.question: IP Source Guard (ip verify source) apoia-se em quê?
options: Na binding table do DHCP snooping (e statics) para permitir só o IP/MAC aprendido naquela porta
pt.explanation: IPSG filtra no data plane o que DAI filtra no ARP. Port-security cobre o MAC; juntos fecham spoofing na borda. Exige snooping ativo e portas trusted rumo ao servidor DHCP.

pt.question: Num fabric SD-Access, qual é o papel do border node versus do edge node?
options: Border só faz Wi-Fi; edge só faz MPLS
Edge conecta endpoints (LISP ETR/ITR, anycast SVI); border liga o fabric ao mundo exterior (fusion, DC, WAN, Internet)
pt.explanation: Control plane node = MS/MR LISP. Edge = access. Border = exit. WLC/FN liga APs. ISE dá SGT. Underlay é IGP/IS-IS + VXLAN; overlay são VN (macro-segmentação) + SGTs (micro).

pt.question: No Cisco SD-WAN, o que é um TLOC e quem distribui as rotas OMP?
options: TLOC é um VLAN tag; OMP corre no vBond apenas
TLOC (Transport Locator) identifica a ligação de um WAN Edge a um transport; o vSmart distribui OMP (rotas, TLOCs, políticas) aos edges
pt.explanation: vBond faz orquestração/STUN inicial. vManage = config/analytics. vSmart = control plane OMP. WAN Edge (vEdge/cEdge) forma túneis IPsec/GRE por TLOC (cor, encaps, system-ip). App-aware routing usa SLA dos túneis.

pt.question: MST (802.1s): o que é a IST (instance 0)?
options: Uma instância por VLAN como no PVST+
A instância que corre BPDUs para a região e mapeia VLANs não noutros instances; liga a região ao CST exterior
pt.explanation: MST agrupa VLANs em poucas instâncias (carga de CPU). Todos os switches da região partilham nome, revisão e mapa VLAN-instance. IST (instance 0) é o 'CIST' dentro da região. PVST simulation nas fronteiras.

pt.question: Storm control num switch de acesso serve para quê?
options: Rate-limitar unicast desconhecido, multicast ou broadcast na porta, evitando que um loop/storm esgote o domínio
pt.explanation: storm-control broadcast/multicast/unicast level X. Pode shutdown ou trap. Complementa BPDU Guard e loop guard mas não substitui STP. Nível em pps ou % da interface.

pt.question: NBAR/AVC em QoS ENCOR classifica tráfego como?
options: Por aplicação (DPI/signatures, PDLM/NAR), permitindo marking/queuing de apps que usam portas dinâmicas
pt.explanation: match protocol na MQC usa NBAR. Útil para SaaS, voice RTP, e apps que não cabem numa ACL. Performance: offload em hardware recente. Não substitui a classificação na trust boundary quando o DSCP já vem correto.

pt.question: Hierarchical QoS (H-QoS) parent/child serve tipicamente para quê?
options: O parent faz shape da interface/túnel (CIR do ISP); o child faz LLQ/CBWFQ dentro dessa fatia
pt.explanation: Numa subinterface ou DMVPN, o parent shaper evita burst contra o policer do ISP; o child dá prioridade à voz (priority) e bandwidth às classes. Sem parent, o TX da interface física (1G) ignora o contrato de 100M.

pt.question: MPLS EXP (Traffic Class) de 3 bits mapeia QoS no núcleo como?
options: Carrega uma classe de serviço no label; o PE copia/mapeia DSCP↔EXP na entrada e o núcleo faz PHB sem olhar para o IP
pt.explanation: Pipe vs uniform vs short-pipe models definem se o DSCP original se restaura no egress. PHP com implicit-null perde EXP no último hop — daí explicit-null quando o PHB no PE de egress importa.

pt.question: OSPF max-metric router-lsa (on-startup) usa-se para quê?
options: Anunciar o LSA Type 1 com métrica máxima durante o boot/reload, desviando o trânsito até os iBGP/MPLS estarem prontos
pt.explanation: Evita blackholes de transito quando o IGP converge antes do BGP (wait-for-bgp). Alternativas: iBGP IGP delay, prefix-suppression, BFD. É o análogo ISIS overload bit.

pt.question: A sincronização BGP (synchronization) no IOS moderno está:
options: Desligada por omissão; quando ligada, um prefixo iBGP só entra na RIB se também for conhecido via IGP
pt.explanation: A regra antiga evitava blackholes em cores que não corriam BGP em todos os hops. Com MPLS/full-mesh/RR e forwarding por labels ou full BGP, synchronization é obsoleta (no synchronization default).

pt.question: Em OSPFv3 com Address Families no IOS-XE, o que permite um único processo?
options: Trocar topologia/LSAs para IPv6 e IPv4 sob o mesmo framework OSPFv3, com AF separadas
Substituir totalmente o BGP na Internet
Desativar o NDP em todos os enlaces
pt.explanation: OSPFv3 AF separa address-family ipv6 e ipv4 unicast. A sessão/adjacência é OSPFv3; os prefixos anunciados dependem da AF ativa.

pt.question: Porque é comum configurar manualmente o router-id em OSPFv3 puro IPv6?
options: Porque o Router ID OSPF continua a ser um valor de 32 bits e pode não haver interface IPv4 de onde o derivar
Porque OSPFv3 exige um IPv6 Router ID de 128 bits
Porque o Router ID tem de ser igual ao MAC
Porque sem router-id o STP não elege root
pt.explanation: Mesmo em IPv6-only, o OSPF Router ID é 32 bits. Sem endereços IPv4, o IOS pode falhar a eleição automática do RID — define-se com router-id A.B.C.D.

en.question: What is the main difference between OSPFv2 and OSPFv3?
options: OSPFv3 is designed for IPv6 and uses link-local addresses for adjacencies
en.explanation: OSPFv3 was redesigned for IPv6, uses link-local addresses to form adjacencies, and supports multiple addresses per interface.

en.question: What is a 'BGP route reflector' and what is its function?
options: Device that reflects BGP routes to reduce full-mesh sessions
en.explanation: A Route Reflector allows a router to reflect BGP routes learned from one client to other clients, reducing the number of required IBGP sessions.

en.question: What is the function of 'EIGRP named mode'?
options: Modern mode that allows hierarchical configuration and named EIGRP for multiple instances
en.explanation: EIGRP named mode allows more organized configuration, support for multiple instances, and advanced features like wide metrics.

en.question: What is 'SD-WAN' and how does it differ from traditional WAN?
options: Software-defined approach to WAN management with intelligent overlay, zero-touch provisioning, and application-aware traffic optimization
en.explanation: SD-WAN uses an intelligent overlay over any underlay (MPLS, internet, LTE) with centralized management and application-based policies.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco DNA Center'?
options: Intent-based automation and network management platform with analytics and assurance
en.explanation: DNA Center provides intent-based automation, automated discovery, policies, and analytics for enterprise networks.

en.question: What is the difference between 'PIM-SM' and 'PIM-DM'?
options: PIM-SM is dense mode, PIM-DM is sparse mode
PIM-SM uses a rendezvous point and is efficient for sparse groups, PIM-DM floods and prunes
en.explanation: PIM-SM (Sparse Mode) uses an RP and is efficient for few receivers. PIM-DM (Dense Mode) floods the network and prunes branches without receivers.

en.question: What is 'EVPN' (Ethernet VPN) in VXLAN environments?
options: Control plane technology for VXLAN that uses BGP to distribute MAC/IP information
en.explanation: EVPN uses BGP as the control plane for VXLAN, enabling efficient distribution of MACs, IPs, and VTEP information.

en.question: What is the function of 'NetFlow' and 'Flexible NetFlow'?
options: Traffic flow monitoring technology for analysis, billing, and security
en.explanation: NetFlow collects flow data for traffic analysis, anomaly detection, and network planning.

en.question: What is 'Cisco TrustSec' and 'SGT'?
options: Security architecture based on tags (Security Group Tags) for identity-based access control
en.explanation: TrustSec uses SGTs (Security Group Tags) to classify traffic and apply identity-based access policies, independent of IP.

en.question: What is the function of 'IPsec' in VPNs?
options: Encrypt traffic at the application layer
Provide network-layer security (confidentiality, integrity, authentication) for VPNs
en.explanation: IPsec operates at the network layer, providing encryption, authentication, and integrity for VPN tunnels.

en.question: What is 'AnyConnect' from Cisco?
options: Secure remote access VPN client with SSL/TLS and IPsec support
en.explanation: Cisco AnyConnect is the modern VPN client that supports SSL VPN and IPsec with advanced mobility features.

en.question: What is the function of a 'Wireless LAN Controller (WLC)'?
options: Centralized device that manages multiple Access Points, roaming, security, and RF
en.explanation: WLC centralizes AP management, enables fast roaming, security policies, and RF optimization.

en.question: What is 'CAPWAP'?
options: Protocol used by WLC to control and manage Access Points (replaces LWAPP)
en.explanation: CAPWAP (Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points) is the standard protocol for communication between WLC and APs.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco ISE' (Identity Services Engine)?
options: Centralized identity-based access control platform, 802.1X, profiling, and policy enforcement
en.explanation: ISE provides NAC (Network Access Control), 802.1X, guest access, device profiling, and dynamic policies.

en.question: What is 'SD-Access' from Cisco?
options: Software-defined access architecture with fabric overlay, underlay, and identity-based policies
en.explanation: SD-Access creates a network fabric with VXLAN/EVPN overlay, automated underlay, and SGT-based policies.

en.question: What is 'Ansible' in Cisco network automation?
options: Agentless automation tool that uses YAML playbooks to configure devices via SSH/NETCONF
en.explanation: Ansible is an open-source agentless tool that uses playbooks to automate network configuration in an idempotent way.

en.question: What is 'MPLS L3 VPN'?
options: Technology that allows multiple customers to share MPLS infrastructure with route isolation via VRF
en.explanation: MPLS L3 VPN uses VRFs on PE routers to isolate routes of different customers while sharing the MPLS infrastructure.

en.question: What is 'Cisco Umbrella'?
options: Cloud-based security service that blocks malicious domains, C2, and phishing via DNS
en.explanation: Umbrella is a cloud DNS security service that blocks threats before they reach the network.

en.question: What is the function of 'Stealthwatch' (now Secure Network Analytics)?
options: Network Detection and Response (NDR) solution that uses machine learning to detect threats and anomalies
en.explanation: Stealthwatch analyzes network flow to detect anomalous behavior and advanced threats.

en.question: What is 'Cisco Secure Firewall' (formerly Firepower)?
options: Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) with IPS, URL filtering, malware protection, and ISE integration
en.explanation: Secure Firewall is an NGFW with deep inspection, IPS, application control, and integration with other Cisco security solutions.

en.question: What is 'Intent-Based Networking'?
options: Approach where you define the 'what' (intent) and the network automatically configures the 'how'
en.explanation: Intent-Based Networking allows administrators to declare business intents and the network automatically translates them into policies and configurations.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco DNA Assurance'?
options: Analytics and proactive troubleshooting with machine learning and real-time telemetry
en.explanation: DNA Assurance uses telemetry, ML, and analytics to identify issues before they affect users and suggest fixes.

en.question: What is 'Zero Trust Security' in Cisco architecture?
options: Never trust, always verify - microsegmentation, continuous identity, and least privilege
en.explanation: Zero Trust assumes nothing is trusted by default and applies continuous verification, microsegmentation, and least-privilege policies.

en.question: What is the difference between 'underlay' and 'overlay' in SD-WAN/SD-Access?
options: Underlay is the physical infrastructure (MPLS, internet), overlay is the virtual network (VXLAN, DMVPN) built on top
en.explanation: Underlay = physical underlying network. Overlay = logical virtual network built on top of the underlay for abstraction and services.

en.question: What is 'Cisco vManage' in SD-WAN?
options: Centralized management controller for policies and orchestration of the entire SD-WAN solution
en.explanation: vManage is the centralized dashboard for management, configuration, policies, and monitoring of the entire SD-WAN fabric.

en.question: What is the function of 'AppQoE' in SD-WAN?
options: Application optimization with application awareness, intelligent QoS, and packet loss correction
en.explanation: AppQoE provides application performance optimization with application awareness and correction techniques.

en.question: What is 'Cisco Umbrella SIG'?
options: Cloud Secure Internet Gateway that combines DNS security, firewall, CASB, and DLP
en.explanation: Umbrella SIG is a cloud secure internet gateway that protects remote and on-premises users.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco Secure Access'?
options: SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) solution that combines networking and security in the cloud
en.explanation: Secure Access is Cisco's SASE solution that provides secure access to any application from anywhere.

en.question: What is 'Cisco XDR' (Extended Detection and Response)?
options: Platform that correlates telemetry from multiple sources (endpoint, network, cloud, email) for advanced threat detection
en.explanation: XDR correlates data from multiple sources for advanced threat detection and response with automation.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco Talos'?
options: Cisco's global threat intelligence team that powers all Cisco security solutions
en.explanation: Talos is Cisco's threat intelligence team that provides real-time data to all Cisco security solutions.

en.question: What is 'Cisco Duo'?
options: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) and adaptive access solution with device health verification
en.explanation: Duo provides MFA, device health verification, and adaptive access to protect logins.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco Secure Endpoint' (formerly AMP for Endpoints)?
options: Advanced endpoint protection with malware detection, EDR, and XDR integration
en.explanation: Secure Endpoint offers real-time protection, threat detection, and response on endpoints.

en.question: What is 'Cisco Secure Email' (formerly ESA)?
options: Secure email gateway with spam, phishing, malware protection, and DLP
en.explanation: Secure Email is Cisco's secure email gateway with advanced protection against email threats.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco Secure Web Appliance' (formerly WSA)?
options: Secure Web Gateway with URL filtering, malware scanning, DLP, and application control
en.explanation: Secure Web Appliance protects web traffic with URL filtering, antimalware, and usage policies.

en.question: What is 'Cisco Meraki'?
options: Cloud-managed networking platform with unified dashboard, zero-touch provisioning, and analytics
en.explanation: Meraki offers switches, APs, firewalls, and cameras 100% cloud-managed with a simple yet powerful dashboard.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco Intersight'?
options: Hybrid infrastructure management platform (data center, edge, cloud) with automation
en.explanation: Intersight provides unified management, automation, and insights for Cisco UCS, HyperFlex, and more infrastructure.

en.question: What is 'Cisco ACI' (Application Centric Infrastructure)?
options: SDN solution for data centers with leaf-spine fabric, application-based policies, and automation
en.explanation: ACI is Cisco's SDN solution for data centers with VXLAN fabric, APIC controller, and application-centric policies.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco Nexus Dashboard'?
options: Management and automation platform for data center with Nexus Dashboard and services
en.explanation: Nexus Dashboard provides unified management, automation, and services for ACI and NX-OS fabrics.

en.question: What is 'Cisco HyperFlex'?
options: Hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) solution with integrated storage, compute, and networking
en.explanation: HyperFlex is Cisco's HCI solution with distributed storage, high availability, and simplified management.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco UCS' (Unified Computing System)?
options: Server platform (blade/rack) with unified management, stateless computing, and automation
en.explanation: UCS integrates compute, networking, and storage with centralized management and stateless service profiles.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco Intersight Workload Optimizer'?
options: AI-powered workload optimization solution for placement, scaling, and cost in hybrid environments
en.explanation: Intersight Workload Optimizer uses AI to optimize workload placement, scaling, and costs across hybrid clouds.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco AppDynamics'?
options: Application observability platform with APM, business transactions, and analytics
en.explanation: AppDynamics provides full-stack visibility into application performance, from code to user experience.

en.question: What is 'Cisco Full-Stack Observability'?
options: Unified approach that correlates data from network, applications, infrastructure, and user experience
en.explanation: Full-Stack Observability correlates telemetry across the entire stack for proactive troubleshooting and optimization.

en.question: What is the function of 'Cisco ThousandEyes' in SD-WAN?
options: Internet and application performance monitoring to optimize SD-WAN decisions
en.explanation: ThousandEyes provides insights into internet and application performance so SD-WAN can make intelligent decisions.

en.question: OSPF LSA type 3 is generated by:
options: The ABR, as an inter-area summary
en.explanation: Type 3 Network Summary is created by the ABR.

en.question: OSPF LSA type 5 represents:
en.explanation: Type 5 AS-External comes from the ASBR (NSSA uses type 7).

en.question: An OSPF stub area blocks which LSAs?
options: Type 5 (externals); the ABR injects a default
en.explanation: Stub does not receive type 5; the ABR advertises 0.0.0.0.

en.question: The EIGRP successor is:
options: The backup route in the topology table
The primary route in the routing table (lowest FD)
The neighbor with the worst metric
en.explanation: Successor is the best route (feasible distance).

en.question: BGP path selection: after Weight and Local Pref, a common next criterion is:
en.explanation: Typical order: Weight, Local Pref, locally originated, shortest AS-Path...

en.question: BGP Weight is:
options: Cisco-proprietary, local to the router, higher is better (default 32768 for originated)
en.explanation: Weight never leaves the router; higher wins.

en.question: In iBGP, a higher Local Preference means:
en.explanation: High Local Pref chooses the AS exit point.

en.question: Default eBGP session TTL is:
en.explanation: eBGP assumes directly connected peers (TTL 1) unless ebgp-multihop.

en.question: iBGP does not re-advertise iBGP prefixes to other iBGP peers. The classic fix is:
options: iBGP full mesh or route reflectors / confederations
en.explanation: iBGP split horizon needs a full mesh or RRs.

en.question: A route-reflector client receives:
options: Routes reflected by the RR, without a client full mesh
en.explanation: The RR relaxes the iBGP mesh among clients.

en.question: VRF-Lite is used to:
options: Separate forwarding tables on the same PE/CE without requiring MPLS
en.explanation: VRFs isolate routing/forwarding; Lite means no MP-BGP/MPLS.

en.question: In MPLS label stacking, the top label is:
options: The L3VPN service label at the bottom
The one the LSR uses for the next hop (transport/IGP)
en.explanation: Top label = transport; bottom (S=1) = VPN service.

en.question: LDP distributes:
en.explanation: LDP maps FECs (prefixes) to labels.

en.question: BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) is used to:
options: Detect forwarding failures in milliseconds, independent of the IGP
en.explanation: BFD gives OSPF/EIGRP/BGP fast failure detection.

en.question: IP SLA on a Cisco router can:
options: Measure latency/jitter/availability and react with tracking
en.explanation: SLA probes plus object tracking for PBR/HSRP/static routes.

en.question: PBR (Policy-Based Routing) steers traffic based on:
options: Route-maps (ACL, DSCP, length) rather than destination alone
en.explanation: PBR sets ip next-hop from policy matches.

en.question: StackWise / StackWise Virtual aggregates:
options: Switches into one logical control plane
en.explanation: The stack is one logical switch with SSO/NSF.

en.question: vPC (Nexus) allows:
options: Two switches to appear as one to STP/LACP without being a single supervisor
en.explanation: vPC is a multi-chassis port-channel without a full stack.

en.question: SD-Access control plane typically uses:
options: LISP to map identity (EID) to location (RLOC)
en.explanation: LISP + VXLAN + ISE in the SDA fabric.

en.question: ISE at the access layer uses 802.1X to:
en.explanation: ISE is the RADIUS policy engine for TrustSec/SDA.

en.question: An SGT (Scalable Group Tag) in TrustSec is:
options: A group tag for identity-based policy
en.explanation: SGTs classify users; SGACLs filter between groups.

en.question: NETCONF typically carries YANG over:
en.explanation: NETCONF/SSH on 830; RESTCONF uses HTTPS.

en.question: A YANG model describes:
options: Structure and constraints of config/state data
en.explanation: YANG is the modeling language for NETCONF/RESTCONF.

en.question: DMVPN Phase 3 allows:
en.explanation: Phase 3: NHRP redirect builds a direct spoke-to-spoke tunnel.

en.question: FlexVPN on IOS-XE is based on:
en.explanation: FlexVPN unifies DMVPN/EasyVPN/RA on IKEv2.

en.question: CoPP (Control Plane Policing) protects:
options: The control-plane CPU by rate-limiting traffic to processes (e.g. SSH, routing)
en.explanation: CoPP applies QoS/ACL to destined-to-box traffic.

en.question: uRPF (unicast RPF) mitigates:
options: Source IP spoofing by checking the source would be routable on the interface
en.explanation: Strict/loose uRPF drops sources inconsistent with the RIB.

en.question: PIM Sparse Mode uses an RP for:
options: The initial shared tree (*,G) before the SPT (S,G)
en.explanation: PIM-SM: join the RP, then it may switch to the shortest-path tree.

en.question: Anycast RP (MSDP) solves:
options: A single RP with no redundancy
Multicast RP redundancy/load-share across boxes or domains
en.explanation: Several RPs share an IP; MSDP syncs source-active state.

en.question: Which OSPFv2 LSA describes a router's links inside the area?
en.explanation: Type 1 is originated by every router and flooded only in the area. Type 2 is from the DR, Type 3 from the ABR, Type 5 from the ASBR.

en.question: What is the difference between an OSPF stub area and an NSSA?
options: Stub blocks Type 5 LSAs and the ABR injects a default; NSSA allows Type 7 (externals from the area) which the ABR translates to Type 5
en.explanation: Totally stubby also blocks Type 3 except a default. Choose NSSA when an ASBR (redistribution) sits inside the edge area.

en.question: What is the initial Cisco BGP Best Path order after next-hop reachability?
options: Highest Weight; then highest Local Preference; locally originated; shortest AS-PATH; origin; lowest MED
Always the peer with the highest IP
en.explanation: Weight (local to the router) is Cisco's first tie-breaker. Local Pref (default 100) is the first attribute advertised in iBGP.

en.question: Which BGP attribute is not advertised to other routers?
en.explanation: Weight is local to the Cisco box and never leaves in an UPDATE. Local Pref travels in iBGP. AS-PATH and MED travel in eBGP.

en.question: In an MPLS L3VPN, what are RD and RT for?
options: They are the same community value
RD makes the prefix unique in VPNv4 BGP; RT (extended community) controls import/export among VRFs
en.explanation: The same IPv4 in two customers needs different RDs. RTs define import/export policy. A VRF can import several RTs (extranet).

en.question: How does VRF-lite differ from MPLS VPN?
options: It separates forwarding tables on the same box without MPLS labels; inter-box links carry one subinterface/VLAN per VRF
en.explanation: VRF-lite is campus/WAN multi-VRF: vrf definition, ip vrf forwarding on the SVI, per-VRF routing, no MPLS core. Overlapping IPs are allowed.

en.question: In EIGRP, what is a Feasible Successor?
options: Always the route in the FIB
A backup route that passes the Feasibility Condition (neighbor AD < successor FD) and can be installed without a DUAL recomputation
en.explanation: Successor = the path in use (lowest FD). Without an FS, a failure goes active and queries. Variance allows unequal-cost load balancing with FS.

en.question: What does the EIGRP variance command do?
options: It allows unequal-cost load balancing among the successor and feasible successors whose FD fits in FD_min × variance
en.explanation: Variance 1 (default) is equal-cost only. Variance 2 installs FS routes with metric up to 2× the successor. K-values must match on neighbors.

en.question: What is the main advantage of MST (802.1s) over Rapid PVST+?
options: MST always runs one tree per VLAN
MST maps many VLANs onto a few instances, cutting BPDUs and CPU when hundreds of VLANs exist
en.explanation: Rapid PVST+ = one instance per VLAN. MST groups VLANs into IST/MSTI with a region (name, revision, map). The digest must match in the region.

en.question: What does UDLD detect?
options: A unidirectional link (TX on one side with no RX on the other) that STP may miss, creating a forwarding loop
en.explanation: UDLD sends frames and expects the peer to echo them. Normal mode syslogs; aggressive errdisables. It complements STP Loop Guard. Typical on fiber.

en.question: What does STP Loop Guard do?
options: It prevents a non-designated port from becoming designated forwarding if BPDUs stop, avoiding a unidirectional loop
en.explanation: If BPDUs stop, classic STP assumes the designated bridge is gone and may forward. Loop Guard puts the port loop-inconsistent until BPDUs return.

en.question: How do SSO and NSF relate on a Cisco chassis with dual RP?
options: NSF saves the config; SSO does not
SSO replicates control-plane state to the standby RP; NSF keeps CEF forwarding during switchover with graceful restart
They are the same NAT feature
en.explanation: SSO + NSF/GR allow supervisor failover in seconds without dropping adjacencies if the peer understands GR. ISSU builds on this.

en.question: What is LLQ (Low Latency Queuing) in a QoS policy-map?
options: A priority queue (usually EF/voice) served first, combined with CBWFQ for the other classes
en.explanation: priority implies a policer so voice cannot starve the link. Other classes use bandwidth (CBWFQ). Do not put bulk traffic in priority.

en.question: DSCP EF 46 as a 6-bit binary value is?
en.explanation: EF = 101110 = 46 decimal. Voice 802.1p CoS is usually 5, mapped to EF at the edge.

en.question: What is WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection) for?
options: Dropping packets probabilistically before the queue fills, by precedence/DSCP, avoiding synchronized TCP tail drops
en.explanation: Tail drop fills the queue and many TCPs hit slow start together. WRED starts dropping earlier on lower-priority flows. Do not apply it to voice.

en.question: What is the fundamental difference between plain GRE and GRE over IPsec?
options: GRE encapsulates any protocol but is clear text; IPsec adds confidentiality/integrity, usually in tunnel mode
en.explanation: GRE alone is protocol 47 with no crypto. IPsec (ESP proto 50) encrypts. For IGP over VPN use GRE/IPsec, VTI, FlexVPN or DMVPN. Lower MTU/MSS.

en.question: What is the main advantage of IKEv2 over IKEv1?
options: Fewer round-trips, native NAT traversal, EAP, MOBIKE, and better rekey; IKEv1 is the legacy model
IKEv1 supports EAP and IKEv2 does not
en.explanation: IKEv2 uses 4 messages versus 9 in main mode. Cisco FlexVPN is built on IKEv2.

en.question: What distinguishes GETVPN from tunnel VPNs such as DMVPN?
options: GETVPN encrypts native traffic (no tunnel overlay) with GDOI group keys; it preserves the original IP header
GETVPN is only for public Internet without an IGP
en.explanation: A key server distributes KEKs/TEKs via GDOI. GMs encapsulate ESP but keep original src/dst. Ideal on a private WAN; it does not traverse NAT like DMVPN.

en.question: What is MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE)?
options: Hop-by-hop Layer 2 encryption between ports, with keys via MKA (802.1X)
en.explanation: Useful on datacenter/campus switch links for confidentiality on the wire. It does not replace WAN IPsec.

en.question: What is MAB (MAC Authentication Bypass) in 802.1X access?
options: A fallback that authenticates the device by MAC via RADIUS when no 802.1X supplicant is present
en.explanation: Typical order: 802.1X, then MAB, then WebAuth. MAB is weak (MACs are spoofable); combine it with profiling and dACL/SGT.

en.question: What is ERSPAN compared with SPAN/RSPAN?
options: It encapsulates monitored traffic in GRE/IP toward an analyzer on another L3 network, crossing routers
en.explanation: SPAN: same switch. RSPAN: a dedicated VLAN across L2 trunks. ERSPAN: GRE/IP, reaches a destination in another subnet.

en.question: What is model-driven telemetry on IOS-XE/NX-OS?
options: Streaming of YANG data (periodic or on-change) via gRPC/gNMI/NETCONF to collectors, instead of SNMP pull
en.explanation: Subscriptions target YANG paths. Second-level cadence and on-change notifications give visibility SNMP cannot scale.

en.question: What is YANG in network programmability?
options: A data modeling language (config and state) used by NETCONF/RESTCONF/gNMI
en.explanation: Modules such as Cisco-IOS-XE-native and openconfig-interfaces describe leaves and types. Encoding may be XML or JSON. Without YANG, NETCONF has no schema.

en.question: What is a practical contrast between NETCONF and RESTCONF?
options: RESTCONF uses only SSH and always XML datastore lock
NETCONF runs over SSH with datastores (running/candidate) and XML RPCs; RESTCONF maps YANG to HTTP/HTTPS with JSON or XML
en.explanation: NETCONF: edit-config, locks, candidate+commit. RESTCONF: GET /restconf/data/... is simpler for web apps. gNMI is the third path.

en.question: In LISP, what are EID and RLOC?
options: EID is the host/prefix identity; RLOC is the location (xTR loopback) used to encapsulate on the underlay
en.explanation: Map-resolver/map-server resolve EID to RLOC. xTRs encapsulate. This is the SD-Access control plane with VXLAN as the data plane.

en.question: What identifies a VXLAN segment in the data plane?
options: The 24-bit VNI (VXLAN Network Identifier) in the VXLAN header, destination UDP 4789
en.explanation: 24 bits ~ 16 million segments (versus 4094 VLANs). VTEPs encapsulate Ethernet in UDP/IP. EVPN distributes MAC/IP to VTEP mappings.

en.question: What is an anycast gateway in a VXLAN/EVPN or SD-Access fabric?
options: Classic HSRP with two different IPs
The same SVI IP and MAC configured on every leaf, so the default gateway is always on the local leaf
en.explanation: The host ARPs the gateway and the local leaf answers. That avoids trombone routing through a central HSRP pair. The underlay provides leaf-to-leaf reachability.

en.question: What timer and DR difference exists between OSPF point-to-point and broadcast?
options: Both elect a DR and use Hello 30
P2P: no DR/BDR, Hello 10 s, direct FULL adjacency; broadcast: elects DR/BDR, Hello 10 s, FULL only with DR/BDR
en.explanation: ip ospf network point-to-point on Ethernet p2p (/31 links) avoids a useless election. A network-type mismatch blocks adjacency.

en.question: What are BGP communities used for?
options: Optional tags that travel with the route so policy (local-pref, filter, no-export) can be applied elsewhere in the AS or at a peering
en.explanation: Well-known: no-export, no-advertise, internet, local-AS. Route-maps set/match community. This is the transit and customer policy tool.

en.question: What is a Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) in IP FRR?
options: A precomputed backup next hop that does not reconverge the prefix through the protected router, allowing sub-50 ms repair
en.explanation: The IGP finds a neighbor whose path to the prefix does not go through the primary. Remote LFA/TI-LFA covers cases with no local LFA. BFD detects the failure.

en.question: How are Private VLANs (PVLAN) organized?
options: One primary VLAN plus secondary isolated VLANs (talk only to promiscuous) or community VLANs (talk among themselves and to promiscuous)
en.explanation: The promiscuous port (gateway/firewall) sees everyone. Isolated hosts do not talk to each other. Community groups hosts. Useful in shared hosting.

en.question: What characterizes a FlexConnect AP versus Local mode?
options: FlexConnect forces all traffic to the WLC
In FlexConnect the AP can switch an SSID locally and survive if CAPWAP to the WLC dies; Local mode uses central switching at the WLC
Local mode does not use CAPWAP
en.explanation: Branches with a weak WAN use FlexConnect: local DHCP/data. Local/centrally switched is the campus model. The WLC still manages RRM while the tunnel is up.

en.question: Which main functions does RRM run on a WLC?
options: TPC (power), DCA (channel selection), and coverage hole detection, tuning RF across the AP group
en.explanation: The WLC measures neighbors (NDP), avoids co-channel interference, raises/lowers dBm, and covers holes. Without RRM, channels and power stay static.

en.question: What does IGMP snooping do on a switch?
options: It watches IGMP joins/leaves and forwards IP multicast only to ports with receivers (and the router/querier)
It enables PIM-DM on every port
en.explanation: Without snooping the switch treats multicast as VLAN broadcast. With snooping plus a querier you save the uplink. MLD snooping is the IPv6 equivalent.

options: Local Preference 200 > 150 (after Weight, which is 0 on both)
Origin e is preferred over i

en.question: Look at this show ip eigrp topology. Is the path via 10.1.3.2 a feasible successor?
options: Yes, because advertised distance 2816 is less than the successor FD (3072)
Yes, because reported metric 3328 is less than 2816
en.explanation: Successor: via 10.1.1.2, FD=3072 (feasible distance = metric to the destination). Candidate via 10.1.3.2: (reported AD=2816, total FD=3328). Feasibility: AD 2816 < successor FD 3072 → it is an FS, but it is not installed (1 successor; variance 1). P = Passive, DUAL is stable.

options: The IGP is down but BFD lingered
The BFD session is up and forwarding to those next hops is considered alive
LD/RD 1/1 means a loop was detected
en.explanation: BFD Up lets OSPF/EIGRP/BGP react in milliseconds without waiting for dead timers. LD/RD are local/remote discriminators. Int is the session interface. Without BFD, Gi0/0 would use 10 s hellos / 40 s dead on OSPF broadcast.

options: There is a single shared forwarding table
Two VRF-Lite instances (CUST_A and CUST_B) with distinct RDs and non-overlapping interfaces
MPLS TE is up on Lo10
Both VRFs must use the same RD
en.explanation: Each VRF has its own RIB/FIB. RD 65000:10 vs 65000:20 distinguishes prefixes if they are exported as VPNv4; in pure VRF-Lite the RD still identifies the VRF. Gi0/0 cannot belong to both VRFs at once.

en.question: Who originates OSPFv2 Type 2 (Network) LSAs and what do they describe?
options: The DR on a multiaccess segment: the list of routers on the segment and the mask
en.explanation: Type 2 exists only where there is a DR (broadcast/NBMA). The Link ID is the DR interface IP. Point-to-point has no Type 2. Type 1 describes the router's own links.

en.question: What is the Type 4 (ASBR-summary) LSA for?
options: To let routers in other areas know how to reach an ASBR (ASBR Router ID, originated by the ABR)
To replace Type 5 inside an NSSA
en.explanation: Type 5 carries the external prefix, but the forwarding next hop may be an ASBR in another area. Type 4 gives the cost to that ASBR. NSSAs do not take Type 5: they use Type 7, translated to 5 at the ABR.

en.question: What extra LSAs does an OSPF totally stubby (no-summary) area block versus a plain stub?
options: Besides Type 4/5, also Type 3 summaries; the ABR injects only a Type 3 default
en.explanation: Stub: no Type 5 (and no Type 4). Totally stubby: no specific Type 3 either, only a default. NSSA: allows redistributed Type 7. Totally NSSA: NSSA plus no-summary. The backbone (area 0) is never stub.

en.question: When do you use an OSPF virtual-link?
options: To attach a discontiguous area to area 0 (or repair a split area 0) through a non-stub transit area
en.explanation: Every area must touch the backbone. A virtual-link is a logical tunnel between ABRs across a regular area. It cannot cross stub/NSSA. The clean fix is to redesign so area 0 is contiguous.

en.question: What is Stuck-in-Active (SIA) in EIGRP?
options: The router stayed Active waiting for Query replies and the SIA timer expired with no reply from a neighbor
en.explanation: With no FS, DUAL sends Queries. If a neighbor never replies (bad WAN, MTU, CPU), the router declares SIA and resets that adjacency. Mitigation: stub, summarization, SIA timer, stable links.

en.question: What does an EIGRP router configured as stub connected summary do?
options: It advertises only connected and summary and is not queried for destinations beyond the stub (reduces SIA)
en.explanation: EIGRP stub is for branches: the hub does not send Queries to the stub asking about core networks. receive-only/static/redistributed are variants. It is not the same as an OSPF stub.

en.question: EIGRP K-values must match between neighbors. Which Ks does the classic default use?
options: K1 through K5 all set to 1
en.explanation: Classic metric ≈ 256 * (10^7/min_bw + sum_delay). K2 (load) and K4/K5 (reliability) are unused by default. Wide metrics (named mode) use 64 bits. K mismatch = no adjacency.

en.question: In BGP, a lower MED (metric) means what, and where is it compared?
options: A worse path; it is always compared across different ASes with no exception
A better path; it is compared among routes from the same neighboring AS (unless bgp always-compare-med)
It is not in best path
en.explanation: MED is optional non-transitive. Cisco by default compares MED only among paths from the same neighbor AS. always-compare-med compares across ASes (and can loop if inconsistent). A missing MED is treated as 0 by default (bgp bestpath med missing-as-worst flips that).

en.question: What is BGP AS-path prepend for?
options: To shorten the path so it always wins
To advertise the prefix with your AS repeated, making the path longer for neighbors and steering inbound traffic away
To force an iBGP full mesh
en.explanation: Prepend is cheap inbound traffic engineering. Local Pref/Weight control outbound. Communities (no-export, local-AS) scale more cleanly. It does not break the AS; it only lengthens the path.

en.question: Why configure neighbor x.x.x.x next-hop-self on iBGP at a PE/edge?
options: So the next hop of eBGP prefixes passed into iBGP is an address reachable in the AS IGP (the speaker itself)
en.explanation: eBGP leaves the next hop as the external peer, often unresolvable in the core. next-hop-self rewrites it to the iBGP peering address (loopback). On an RR it applies toward clients. Alternative: advertise the external next-hop /32 in the IGP (usually undesirable).

en.question: What does the well-known community no-export mean?
options: Do not advertise the prefix to any iBGP peer
Do not advertise the prefix outside the AS (nor from a confederation to 'real' eBGP)
en.explanation: no-export: stay inside the AS. no-advertise: do not advertise to any peer. local-AS: do not leave the confederation sub-AS. internet (default) may go to everyone. Communities are the ISP policy hook.

en.question: What is the difference between a BGP route reflector and a confederation?
options: An RR relaxes iBGP split-horizon inside a cluster (clients/non-clients); a confederation splits the AS into sub-ASes with special eBGP between them
en.explanation: Both avoid a full iBGP mesh. RR is simpler (cluster-id, originator-id against loops). A confederation (private 64512-65534) isolates policy per sub-AS and treats inter-sub-AS like eBGP for next-hop/MED. They can be combined.

en.question: What is eBGP multihop?
options: Allowing an eBGP session between addresses that are not directly adjacent by raising TTL (default eBGP TTL is 1)
en.explanation: Typical: peering between loopbacks across a shared IGP/connected network, or peering several hops away. disable-connected-check covers loopbacks on the same link. Risk: a large TTL widens the attack surface; BFD is still recommended.

en.question: In an MPLS L3VPN, where does PHP (penultimate hop popping) happen?
options: On the router immediately before the egress PE, which pops the transport label (LDP/SR)
en.explanation: The transport LSP is LDP (or SR). The penultimate hop pops so the egress PE looks only at the VPN label (or IP, with PHP vs explicit-null variations). explicit-null preserves EXP/TTL to the egress.

en.question: LDP versus RSVP-TE in MPLS: which contrast is correct?
options: LDP builds LSPs from the IGP RIB, hop by hop; RSVP-TE signals tunnels with bandwidth/path constraints
en.explanation: LDP rides beside the IGP (UDP 646 hello, TCP 646 session). RSVP-TE (and SR-TE) is for engineering: bandwidth, affinity, fast reroute. Many cores mix LDP at the edge with TE in the backbone, or move to Segment Routing.

en.question: BFD echo mode versus asynchronous: what is the idea?
options: Echo does not exist on Cisco
Async: both peers send control packets; Echo: the peer loops the initiator's echo packet on the forwarding path
en.explanation: Echo tests the neighbor data plane with less CPU on the peer. Not all hardware/IOS supports echo. 50x3 ms timers are common on LAN; WAN uses more conservative values. BFD is tied to IGP/BGP with fall-over bfd / bfd all-interfaces.

en.question: In PBR, what is the difference between set ip next-hop and set interface?
options: set ip next-hop uses an IP (falling back to normal routing if unreachable, unless default); set interface forces that outbound iface (dangerous on multiaccess without ARP)
set interface works only with BGP
set ip next-hop ignores the route-map ACL
en.explanation: PBR (ip policy route-map) matches ACLs/length/DSCP and steers before the RIB. set ip next-hop verify-availability plus tracking/BFD avoids black holes. set ip default next-hop applies only when the RIB has no route (except default).

en.question: In Nexus vPC, what are the peer-link and peer-keepalive for?
options: Peer-link syncs state (MCS, LACP, IGMP, BPDUs) between the two peers; keepalive (separate, often mgmt) detects dual-active if the peer-link fails
en.explanation: Servers see one EtherChannel toward two chassis. Without keepalive, a peer-link failure can split-brain (both active). Orphan ports attach to only one peer. STP is handled specially on vPC.

en.question: What is an orphan port in a vPC?
options: An LACP port bundled on both peers
A port that attaches a device to only one of the vPC switches, not to the pair
en.explanation: If the peer hosting the orphan fails, the device loses connectivity even if the other side's vPC is up. Mitigation: dual-attach (vPC) or orphan-port suspend. Peer-gateway / orphan-port may be needed for routed traffic.

en.question: In LISP as used by SD-Access, what does the Map-Server/Map-Resolver do?
options: It encapsulates VXLAN on the data plane of every edge
Control plane: it stores EID→RLOC mappings and answers Map-Requests from ITR/ETR (edges)
en.explanation: The ITR asks 'where is this EID?'; the MS/MR (control-plane node) replies with the ETR's RLOC. The data plane is VXLAN (UDP 4789) between RLOCs. Border nodes connect the fabric to the rest of the network.

en.question: Which UDP port does VXLAN use in the data plane?
en.explanation: VXLAN uses UDP 4789 (IANA). CAPWAP uses 5246/5247. BGP is 179. LDP is 646. The 24-bit VNI identifies the segment in the VXLAN header; EVPN (BGP AF) distributes MAC/IP (RT-2) and prefixes (RT-5).

en.question: Inline SGT versus SXP in TrustSec/ISE: what is the difference?
options: SXP encapsulates VXLAN; inline uses RADIUS
Inline carries the tag in CMD/Cisco Meta Data hop by hop; SXP (TCP 64999) advertises IP-SGT out of band where the media cannot carry the tag
en.explanation: ISE classifies the user and pushes the SGT to the NAD (802.1X). Capable switches forward the tag. SXP fills gaps (WAN, third-party). Enforcement is SGACL at the destination. pxGrid shares context with firewalls.

en.question: What is the NETCONF candidate datastore for?
options: To replace running immediately with no lock
To edit a proposed config (edit-config) and then atomically commit to running, with lock and rollback
en.explanation: candidate plus commit lets you validate and apply all-or-nothing (confirmed-commit with automatic rollback). running-only devices edit live. RESTCONF uses the same YANG model over HTTP. Confirmed commit is the antidote to AAA/ACL lockouts.

en.question: DMVPN Phase 1 versus Phase 3: which contrast is correct?
options: Phase 1 is hub-and-spoke (spokes do not build tunnels to each other); Phase 3 uses NHRP redirect/shortcut for spoke-to-spoke
en.explanation: Phase 2 allows spoke-to-spoke but needs full routing tables on spokes (hub summaries break it). Phase 3: the hub sends NHRP redirect, spokes install shortcuts; hub summaries work. IPsec profile + mGRE + NHRP are common to all phases.

en.question: In GETVPN, what are the Key Server (KS) and Group Member (GM) roles?
options: KS forwards the data plane; GM only runs the IGP
KS distributes group SAs (GDOI/IKEv1) to GMs; GMs encrypt the original traffic while preserving the IP header (tunnel-less) on the private WAN
en.explanation: GETVPN (GDOI) fits private/MPLS WANs where the original IP header must remain for routing. TBAR (time-based anti-replay) and COOP KS (redundancy) are typical. It does not replace DMVPN on the public Internet (no group tunnel/NAT traversal).

en.question: CoPP versus CPPr (Control Plane Protection): what is the nuance?
options: They are the same feature with no difference
CoPP applies a policy-map to the logical control-plane interface (aggregate); CPPr (host/transit/cef-exception) further splits CEF for extra granularity on classic IOS
en.explanation: Both protect CPU from floods (TTL expiry, ICMP, SSH). Start from a Cisco-recommended policy and tune. Undercopping breaks BGP/OSPF; over-permitting lets DoS in. NX-OS uses copp profile.

en.question: uRPF strict versus loose: what is the difference?
options: Loose requires the source to match the ingress interface; strict only requires the prefix in the FIB
Strict: the source reverse path must point at the ingress interface; loose: the source just has to exist in the FIB (any iface), useful with asymmetry
en.explanation: ip verify unicast source reachable-via rx = strict; reachable-via any = loose. Strict is strong anti-spoofing at access; loose at the edge with asymmetric routing. allow-default and an exception ACL tune behavior.

en.question: On a PIM-SM multiaccess segment, what is the Designated Router (DR) for?
options: Sending Registers to the RP (sources) and Join/Prune on behalf of local receivers (IGMP)
en.explanation: The PIM DR (highest IP, or priority) is the only router that registers sources and sends joins toward the RP. Do not confuse it with the OSPF DR. Assert elects the forwarder when several routers have the same group on a LAN.

en.question: What is the contrast between Auto-RP and BSR for RP discovery?
options: BSR is Cisco-only; Auto-RP is IETF
Auto-RP (Cisco, 224.0.1.39/40) advertises RPs via a mapping agent; BSR (RFC, PIM messages) elects a Bootstrap Router that floods the RP-set
en.explanation: Auto-RP needs sparse-dense or auto-rp listener so groups 39/40 can flow. BSR is the standard and rides native PIM-SM. Anycast-RP (MSDP or RFC 4610) gives geographic RP redundancy.

en.question: What is SPT switchover in PIM-SM?
options: After the first packet arrives on the shared tree (*,G) toward the RP, the last-hop DR may send an (S,G) Join toward the source, taking the RP off the path
en.explanation: Cisco defaults to immediate switchover (spt-threshold 0). spt-threshold infinity keeps traffic on the shared tree (useful for brief sources). SSM (IGMPv3, 232/8) goes (S,G) with no RP.

en.question: IS-IS in ENCOR campus/WAN: what do L1 versus L2 mean?
options: L1 is eBGP; L2 is iBGP
L1 is intra-area (station); L2 is the backbone between areas; L1/L2 sits at the border and leaks a default
en.explanation: IS-IS has no OSPF-style area 0: the backbone is the contiguous set of L2 routers. NET is area + SysID + NSEL. Wide metric is required on modern networks. IS-IS is a common SR/LDP base in SPs.

en.question: What do OSPFv3 Address Families (AF) on IOS-XE allow?
options: Only a classic IPv6 process with no IPv4
One OSPFv3 process carrying IPv6 and/or IPv4 (AFs), with adjacencies still on link-local
en.explanation: Classic OSPFv3 was IPv6-only. AF (RFC 5838) carries IPv4 over OSPFv3. Adjacencies remain IPv6 link-local; router-id is still a 32-bit IPv4 value. Instance ID separates AFs.

en.question: What is IPv6 RA Guard at the access layer for?
options: Stopping a malicious host from sending Router Advertisements and impersonating an IPv6 gateway
en.explanation: RA Guard (plus DHCPv6 Guard and ND inspection) is First-Hop Security. Access ports: host-mode (RAs dropped). Uplinks to routers: router-mode. Without it, a fake RA steals IPv6 traffic.

en.question: What does IP Source Guard (ip verify source) rely on?
options: The DHCP snooping binding table (plus statics) to allow only the IP/MAC learned on that port
en.explanation: IPSG filters on the data plane what DAI filters in ARP. Port-security covers MAC; together they close edge spoofing. It needs snooping enabled and trusted ports toward the DHCP server.

en.question: In an SD-Access fabric, what is the border node versus the edge node?
options: Border is Wi-Fi only; edge is MPLS only
Edge connects endpoints (LISP ETR/ITR, anycast SVI); border connects the fabric to the outside world (fusion, DC, WAN, Internet)
en.explanation: Control-plane node = LISP MS/MR. Edge = access. Border = exit. WLC/FN attaches APs. ISE provides SGTs. Underlay is IGP/IS-IS plus VXLAN; overlay is VNs (macro-segmentation) plus SGTs (micro).

en.question: In Cisco SD-WAN, what is a TLOC and who distributes OMP routes?
options: A TLOC is a VLAN tag; OMP runs on vBond only
A TLOC (Transport Locator) identifies a WAN Edge's attachment to a transport; vSmart distributes OMP (routes, TLOCs, policies) to the edges
A TLOC is the vManage GUI
en.explanation: vBond does initial orchestration/STUN. vManage is config/analytics. vSmart is the OMP control plane. WAN Edge (vEdge/cEdge) builds IPsec/GRE tunnels per TLOC (color, encaps, system-ip). App-aware routing uses per-tunnel SLA.

en.question: In MST (802.1s), what is the IST (instance 0)?
options: One instance per VLAN as in PVST+
The instance that carries BPDUs for the region and maps VLANs not in other instances; it joins the region to the external CST
en.explanation: MST groups VLANs into a few instances (CPU load). Every switch in the region shares name, revision, and VLAN-instance map. IST (instance 0) is the CIST inside the region. PVST simulation runs at the boundaries.

en.question: What is storm control on an access switch for?
options: Rate-limiting unknown unicast, multicast, or broadcast on the port so a loop/storm cannot exhaust the domain
en.explanation: storm-control broadcast/multicast/unicast level X. It can shut or trap. It complements BPDU Guard and loop guard but does not replace STP. The level is pps or a percent of interface bandwidth.

en.question: How does NBAR/AVC classify traffic in ENCOR QoS?
options: By application (DPI/signatures, PDLM/NAR), allowing marking/queuing of apps that use dynamic ports
en.explanation: match protocol in MQC uses NBAR. Useful for SaaS, RTP voice, and apps that do not fit an ACL. Performance: hardware offload on recent platforms. It does not replace trust-boundary classification when DSCP is already correct.

en.question: What is hierarchical QoS (H-QoS) parent/child typically for?
options: The parent shapes the interface/tunnel (ISP CIR); the child runs LLQ/CBWFQ inside that slice
en.explanation: On a subinterface or DMVPN, the parent shaper prevents bursting into the ISP policer; the child gives voice priority (priority) and bandwidth to other classes. Without a parent, the 1G physical TX ignores a 100M contract.

en.question: How do the 3 MPLS EXP (Traffic Class) bits carry QoS in the core?
options: They carry a class of service in the label; the PE maps DSCP↔EXP at ingress and the core applies PHB without inspecting IP
They exist only with IPv6 LDP
en.explanation: Pipe vs uniform vs short-pipe models decide whether the original DSCP is restored at egress. PHP with implicit-null loses EXP at the last hop — hence explicit-null when the egress PE PHB matters.

en.question: What is OSPF max-metric router-lsa (on-startup) for?
options: Forcing the router to become DR
Advertising Type-1 LSAs with maximum metric during boot/reload, steering transit away until iBGP/MPLS are ready
Turning the area into an NSSA
en.explanation: It avoids transit black holes when IGP converges before BGP (wait-for-bgp). Alternatives: iBGP IGP delay, prefix-suppression, BFD. It is the analogue of the IS-IS overload bit.

en.question: BGP synchronization on modern IOS is:
options: Off by default; when enabled, an iBGP prefix is installed in the RIB only if it is also known via the IGP
en.explanation: The old rule avoided black holes in cores that did not run BGP on every hop. With MPLS/full-mesh/RR and label or full-BGP forwarding, synchronization is obsolete (no synchronization is the default).

en.question: With OSPFv3 Address Families on IOS-XE, what can one process do?
options: Exchange topology/LSAs for IPv6 and IPv4 under the OSPFv3 framework, with separate AFs
Fully replace BGP on the Internet
en.explanation: OSPFv3 AF splits address-family ipv6 and ipv4 unicast. Adjacency is OSPFv3; which prefixes are advertised depends on the active AF.

en.question: Why is a manual router-id common on pure IPv6 OSPFv3?
options: Because the OSPF Router ID is still a 32-bit value and there may be no IPv4 interface to derive it from
Because OSPFv3 requires a 128-bit IPv6 Router ID
Because the Router ID must equal the MAC
Because without a router-id STP cannot elect a root
en.explanation: Even in IPv6-only networks the OSPF Router ID is 32 bits. With no IPv4 addresses, IOS may fail automatic RID election — set it with router-id A.B.C.D.
